en.title: What Is an AI Voice Agent for Garages and Dealerships?
en.description: An AI voice agent answers a workshop's phone, understands the caller and completes the task: booking, status, routing. How it works and what to check first.
en.body:
## Monday, 8:05 AM

Three customers are at the counter with their keys. A technician is waiting at the parts window. The phone has rung four times in ten minutes. Two of those callers gave up. One of them wanted to book a brake job.

That scene is the reason AI voice agents exist for this trade. The counter cannot be in two places. The phone has always lost.

## The definition

An AI voice agent is software that answers the phone in a natural voice, understands what the caller wants in their own words, looks up the answer in the workshop's own systems and completes the task on the call. Booking a service. Moving an appointment. Telling a customer the car is being washed and will be ready from 4 PM. Taking a breakdown call and getting it to the mechanic on duty with a summary.

It is not a menu that asks you to press 1. It is not a recording. It is not an answering service that writes down a message for someone to return tomorrow. The difference is that a voice agent finishes the job while the caller is still on the line.

## How it works, step by step

1. **The call arrives.** The workshop forwards its existing number: all calls, only overflow, or only outside opening hours. The number does not change.
2. **The agent listens.** Speech recognition turns the caller's words into text. A language model works out the intent: "my check engine light came on this morning" is a diagnostic booking, not a general question.
3. **It checks the systems.** Availability comes from the planner or dealer management system. Car-ready status comes from the job card. Prices come from the workshop's own price list.
4. **It acts within the rules.** Job durations, which technician does timing belts, when a loaner car is offered and what counts as a breakdown are set by the workshop manager and approved before go-live.
5. **It confirms.** The booking is written to the planner, read back to the caller and confirmed by text.
6. **It hands off when it should.** A warranty dispute, a complaint or a diagnosis question goes to a person, with the transcript and a summary attached.
7. **It logs everything.** Every call is transcribed, tagged and written to the customer record.

## Why the phone matters more than it looks

Most service work still starts with a call. In a CDK Global survey of more than 2,500 service customers, published in 2025, 64 percent booked their last appointment by phone and 19 percent booked online.

That phone is answered unevenly. Marchex, which analyzes calls for large multi-location automotive service operators, puts missed or failed calls at up to 21 percent, with the best-performing locations still near 10 percent.

The people who could answer are scarce. The TechForce Foundation's 2026 supply and demand report counts about 70,000 automotive technician openings a year in the US against roughly 42,000 graduates.

And the volume is large. NADA reports that US franchised dealerships wrote more than 276 million repair orders in 2025, about 16,252 per dealership, with an average of 16 technicians each. Every one of those repair orders started with a conversation and generated a few more: is it booked, is it ready, what will it cost.

## What a voice agent should and should not do

It should handle the routine: bookings, reschedules, opening hours, car-ready status, tire storage, quotes read from the system, recalls, reminders and no-show calls.

It should not diagnose a fault, promise a repair it cannot see, quote a price that is not in the system or argue with an upset customer. Those go to a person. A good agent knows the line and transfers early, with context, rather than late, with an apology.

## What it looks like in a real garage

Autobedrijf van Nuland, a family garage in Volkel in the Netherlands, forwarded its number to Nekaf after a third of calls went unanswered at peak times and after 5 PM. In the first month every call was answered, more than six in ten were completed without staff, and bookings rose by 23 percent. Those are one garage's numbers, measured on 8,420 calls. Yours will differ, so measure your own missed rate first.

## What to check before you choose one

- **Does it speak the trade?** It should know a timing belt from a tire swap and book the right duration.
- **Does it write to your systems?** Look for your planner or DMS by name: Autoflex, Autotaal, WinCar, Tekmetric, Shopmonkey, Keyloop, CDK Global and so on.
- **Who approves the rules?** You should, before go-live, and every change should be versioned.
- **How does it hand off?** Warm transfer with a summary, not a voicemail.
- **Can you see it work before it goes live?** A shadow period on real calls, scored, is the honest test.
- **Where does the data live?** EU or US residency, encryption and an audit trail.
- **How long to go live?** Days, on your existing number, not a migration project.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do callers know they are talking to software?

They should. A well-configured agent introduces itself, says the call may be recorded and hands over to a person whenever the caller asks.

### Does it need a systems integration to start?

No. A voice agent can run standalone on a forwarded number and a calendar. Nekaf, for example, goes live that way and adds the planner or DMS connection later without interrupting the phones.

en.title: AI in Automotive Aftersales: A Complete Guide (2026)
en.description: Where AI is used across service, parts, tires and body repair in 2026, what the market and labor numbers say, and how a workshop should start.
en.body:
## The first cold Saturday in October

A two-branch tire and fast-fit center opens at 8 AM. By 10 AM there have been forty calls. Half of them ask the same question: can I get my winter set fitted before the weekend. In Germany the "O bis O" rule, October to Easter, sends most of the country to the workshop in the same four weeks, and ADAC and the tire trade association BRV tell drivers every autumn to book early because workshops are full. Every call the counter cannot take is a set of tires fitted somewhere else.

Aftersales is full of moments like this: predictable peaks, thin staffing and a phone that decides who gets the work. This guide covers where AI is used in 2026, what the numbers say and how to start.

## The market, in numbers

- The US light-duty aftermarket reached about $435 billion in 2025 and is forecast by the Auto Care Association and MEMA to grow 5.2 percent in 2026 and pass $500 billion by 2029.
- In the EU, the parts market is around 118 billion euros, of which the independent aftermarket supplies about 73 billion, according to the FIGIEFA and Roland Berger Panorama, which counts around 250,000 independent workshops and outlets.
- Cars are getting older. ACEA puts the EU fleet at 256 million cars with an average age of 12.7 years. S&P Global Mobility puts the US average at 12.8 years.
- Germany's ZDK counts 84,000 companies and 705,000 employees in the motor trade. Dutch workshops did a record 8.19 million periodic inspections on passenger cars in 2025, according to the RDW.

Older cars need more work. The constraint is not demand. It is people.

## The people constraint

The TechForce Foundation's 2026 report estimates that US employers need about 241,842 new technicians a year through 2029 and that schools produce 101,743. For automotive alone it is 70,000 openings against roughly 42,000 graduates. The ZDK has reported a shortfall of around 10,000 skilled workers in the German trade. UWV counted 7,700 open vacancies in the Dutch car sector in the second quarter of 2026, with mechanics, body repairers, painters and receptionists all scarce.

That is why AI in aftersales is mostly about time: taking work off the counter and the shop floor that does not need a trained person. Diagnosis, warranty judgment and angry customers stay with people.

## Where AI is being used

### 1. Customer contact

Voice agents answer the phone, understand the request and complete it: bookings, reschedules, opening hours, car-ready status, tire storage questions. The same rules run on web chat, email, SMS and WhatsApp. The phone is still the main channel: 64 percent of service customers in a 2025 CDK Global survey booked by phone, 19 percent online.

### 2. Scheduling and capacity

Booking the right job type with the right duration and technician, filling canceled slots from a waitlist, calling no-shows within hours and rebooking them, and finding every car due for a service, an inspection or a seasonal tire change and calling until it is booked. Vendor benchmarks such as AutoAlert's put dealership service no-shows at around 20 percent.

### 3. Status and proactive communication

Outbound car-ready calls and texts, parts-arrived updates and repair status for body shops. In Cox Automotive's 2025 Service Industry Study, 45 percent of dealership service customers had a frustration, most often that service took longer than expected. Most status calls exist because nobody told the customer.

### 4. Quotes, approvals and follow-up

Chasing open quotes, answering the questions and turning approvals into bookings. Cox reports that customers are 49 percent more likely to approve recommended work when they see photos or video.

### 5. Claims and estimates

For body shops, checking claims for missing photos, parts and approvals before they reach the insurer. Enterprise Mobility measured the average collision rental at 16.3 days in the first quarter of 2026, with a scheduling backlog of 1.8 weeks. CCC's Crash Course 2026 found that 28.3 percent of repairable estimates now include calibrations.

### 6. Asking questions of your own data

Plain-language questions over the planner and the call log: no-shows per location, unanswered calls last week, cars waiting on parts. Cox Automotive found 16 percent of consumers used AI tools during their service journey in 2026. Workshops can do the same with their own numbers. Ask Nekaf, for example, is free for 90 days and produces a baseline of six access metrics before any agent is switched on.

## How to start

1. Measure first. Answer rate, speed of answer, abandonment, booking accuracy, calls per advisor, after-hours volume and bay utilization.
2. Pick one job. Usually the service desk, because that is where the leak is.
3. Write the rules down. Job durations, technician skills, loaner cars, breakdown handling. The workshop manager approves them.
4. Run in shadow mode. A week on real calls without acting, scored, before anything goes live.
5. Keep the number and the systems. Forward, do not migrate. Connect the planner when ready.
6. Review weekly. Sampled calls, hand-off quality, corrections tested before they go live. Add the next agent only when the first one reports results you can check.

## Governance

Every call transcribed, every decision logged with the rule version that produced it, data held in the EU or the US as required, and a supervising review of sampled conversations. In Europe the EU AI Act and GDPR require it. It is good practice everywhere.

en.title: AI in the Dealership Service Department: A Complete Guide (2026)
en.description: What AI can do in a dealership service department in 2026: the service desk, status calls, recalls, no-shows, DMS integration and what to measure.
en.body:
## A Tuesday in the service lane

Ten cars are booked for 8 AM drop-off. Two customers are waiting for a loaner that is not back yet. A Golf has been on the lift since yesterday waiting on a part, and its owner has called twice. The advisor on the phone is the same advisor writing up the ten cars. By 9:15 the phone has gone to voicemail four times.

The service department is the most profitable part of a dealership and the part with the least slack. This guide covers what AI can do about that in 2026, what the numbers say and where to be careful.

## The numbers

- NADA's 2025 data: 16,990 US franchised dealers wrote more than 276 million repair orders and $164.6 billion in service and parts sales. The average dealership wrote 16,252 repair orders, roughly 65 a working day, with 16 technicians and $494 per customer repair order.
- Cox Automotive's 2026 Fixed Ops and Ownership Study puts average service and parts revenue at about $9.23 million per dealership, up 33 percent over eight years. In the same study, the dealer share of service visits fell from 33 to 29 percent.
- Intent is not the problem. 80 percent of new-car buyers say they are likely to service at the selling dealership. Only about a quarter leave with a first service appointment booked.
- Experience is. In Cox's 2025 Service Industry Study, 45 percent of customers had a frustration with their dealership visit. Among them, the top ones were service taking longer than expected (24 percent), finding out what the dealership charges (13 percent), being pushed toward additional services (13 percent) and a final price above the estimate (12 percent).
- 88 percent say the service experience affects whether they buy from that dealer again.

Every one of these frustrations is a communication problem before it is a workshop problem. That is the part AI can carry.

## Where AI fits

### The service desk

A voice agent answers every call on the first ring, including fifty at once on a Monday morning. It books the right service with the right duration and advisor, moves and cancels appointments and answers hours, directions and price-list questions. Anything unusual goes to an advisor with a transcript and a summary. Marchex, which analyzes calls for multi-location automotive operators, reports missed or failed call rates of up to 21 percent, so the first effect is usually simple: calls that used to ring out now book.

### Car-ready and parts status

The largest single source of inbound calls in most service departments is "is my car ready?" An agent that reads the repair order status can answer it, or better, call or text the customer the moment the job closes. The Golf owner waiting on a part gets told when the part arrives, not when he asks.

### Recalls and campaigns

Manufacturer recalls and service campaigns booked from the vehicle list without a call sheet, at the right duration, with the right parts flagged.

### No-show recovery and the waitlist

Vendor benchmarks put dealership service no-shows around 20 percent, according to AutoAlert, with Dealer1 Solutions reporting show rates of 78 to 82 percent across the dealer networks it sees. An agent calls every no-show within two hours and rebooks, and offers canceled slots to the waitlist until they are filled. Nekaf's no-show recovery agent reports the bay time it recovered, which is the number a service manager actually wants.

### Estimates and approvals

Chasing open estimates by call, text or email and capturing approvals. Cox found customers 49 percent more likely to approve recommended work when they can see photos or video.

### Post-repair follow-up

A call to every customer after the visit, asking the dealer's own questions and flagging problems before they become a survey score.

## The DMS question

None of this is useful if bookings do not land in the dealer system. Look for two-way integration with what you run: Keyloop, CDK Global, Reynolds and Reynolds, Dealertrack, Xtime or incadea. The safe pattern is calendar first, so bookings finish in your own system from day one, then the DMS connection, with every write read back before it is confirmed to the customer. Nekaf, for example, runs standalone on a forwarded number and adds the DMS sync when the dealer is ready.

## Manufacturer standards and CSI

Brand standards for greeting, disclosure and escalation can be written into the rules and versioned. A supervising review that scores sampled calls on accuracy and tone gives the service manager something a call log never did: evidence.

## What to measure

1. Answer rate and speed of answer, per site and per hour.
2. Abandonment rate, especially on hold.
3. Booking accuracy: right job, right duration, right advisor.
4. Calls per advisor per day.
5. After-hours volume and what happens to it.
6. Bay utilization and no-show rate.

Measure them before anything goes live. Cox Automotive also found that 16 percent of consumers used AI tools during their service journey in 2026. Customers are already there. The question is whether the dealership's phone is.

## Where to be careful

- Warranty disputes, complaints and diagnosis stay with people.
- Rules must be approved by the service manager, not by the vendor.
- Run a shadow week on real calls before switching anything on.
- Keep the data in the region your group requires and keep the audit trail.

en.title: What Is an AI Receptionist for a Garage?
en.description: An AI receptionist is a voice agent that runs a garage's front desk by phone: answering, booking, status and hand-offs. What it does and how to set it up.
en.body:
## Friday, 4:55 PM

The owner is under a car with a seized caliper. The phone rings. It is the third call in five minutes. The first two went to voicemail, and one of them was a customer who wanted to book an inspection for Monday. In a one-counter garage the receptionist is whoever is nearest the phone, and on a Friday afternoon that is nobody.

An AI receptionist exists for that garage.

## The definition

An AI receptionist is a voice agent that does the front-desk job on the phone. It answers on the first ring, greets the caller with the garage's name, works out what they need and completes the routine tasks: booking, rescheduling, canceling, opening hours, directions, car-ready status, what a quote covered and when the winter set can be fitted. When a call needs a person, it transfers with a summary so the customer never repeats themselves.

It is not a menu. It is not voicemail. It is not an answering service that takes a message for you to return on Monday. The receptionist finishes the call.

## A day with one

- **7:40 AM.** A caller wants to move Tuesday's oil service to Thursday. The agent checks the planner, offers 9:40 with Marco and confirms by text.
- **8:15 AM.** Six calls in four minutes. All answered. Three bookings, two car-ready questions read from the job cards, one directions question.
- **11:30 AM.** "My check engine light came on and the car feels sluggish." The agent books a diagnostic slot the same afternoon and notes the symptom on the job.
- **2:10 PM.** A customer disputes an invoice. The agent apologizes, takes the details and transfers to the owner with a summary.
- **6:30 PM.** Closed. A caller books an inspection for Monday. Nobody at the garage hears the phone, and nothing is lost.

## Why garages are looking at this now

Phone calls are still how most service work is booked. CDK Global's survey of more than 2,500 service customers, published in 2025, found 64 percent booked by phone and 19 percent online.

Those calls are missed more often than owners think. Marchex data from multi-location automotive operators puts missed or failed calls at up to 21 percent, with the best locations still near 10 percent. Before it forwarded its number, Autobedrijf van Nuland, a family garage in the Netherlands, saw a third of calls go unanswered at peak times and after 5 PM, and half the people who reached voicemail never called back.

The people who could answer are scarce. UWV, the Dutch public employment service, lists receptionists among the occupations the car trade cannot fill, next to mechanics, body repairers and painters, with 7,700 open vacancies in the sector in the second quarter of 2026. The TechForce Foundation counts about 70,000 automotive technician openings a year in the US against 42,000 graduates. Pulling a technician off the lift to answer the phone is the most expensive way to run a front desk.

And there is more competition for the same driver. Cox Automotive counts nearly 299,000 auto mechanic businesses in the US, up 12 percent since 2018. The garage that answers gets the job.

## What it does not do

It does not diagnose. It does not quote a price that is not in the system. It does not decide whether a repair is covered by warranty. It does not argue. Those calls go to a person, early, with context. A good receptionist knows what it does not know.

## Setting one up

1. **Forward the number.** All calls, overflow only, or only when closed. It works with RingCentral, Zoom Phone, Twilio, Vonage, a PBX or a plain SIP trunk. The number stays the same.
2. **Set the rules.** Opening hours, bays, technicians and what each of them does, job durations, loaner cars, what counts as a breakdown and who gets it.
3. **Connect the planner when ready.** Autoflex, Autotaal, WinCar, CarSys, Werbas or Loco-Soft in the Netherlands and Germany; Tekmetric, Shopmonkey, Shop-Ware, AutoLeap, Mitchell 1 or Protractor in the US. A calendar is enough to start.
4. **Listen before you switch on.** A week in shadow mode on real calls shows what it would have said. Nekaf scores those calls with a supervising Reviewer before the owner signs off, and billing starts the day it goes live.
5. **Review weekly.** Read the flagged calls, correct a rule in plain language and let the fix be tested before it goes live.

## What it costs

Nekaf's plans start at $299 a month, with no per-minute or per-seat charges. Compare that with one missed brake job. If your garage takes 500 calls a month and misses a fifth of them, that is 100 callers, and some of them wanted to book.

## Frequently asked questions

### Will customers accept it?

They accept being answered. The agent says what it is, and a person is one sentence away.

### What if it makes a mistake?

Every call is transcribed. Mark the call as wrong, the rule gets fixed and tested, and the customer gets a call back from a person.

### Can it handle Dutch and English on the same line?

Yes. English, Dutch, German and Spanish, set per location.

en.title: What Is Automated Service Booking and Intake for Workshops?
en.description: Automated booking puts the right job in the right bay. Automated intake collects mileage, symptoms and photos before the car arrives. How both work.
en.body:
## 7:30 AM, twelve keys on the counter

Twelve cars are due in before 9. The advisor has a key, a name and a phone number for each. Mileage: unknown. The reason for the visit on four of the job cards reads "noise". Two customers booked forty-five minutes for what will be a three-hour job. The tenth car needs a part that could have been ordered last week.

Booking and intake decide how a workshop day goes before the first bolt is turned. Automating them is less about speed and more about getting the right information into the planner early.

## Two jobs, one flow

**Automated booking** takes a request, by phone, web chat, email or WhatsApp, and turns it into the right appointment: the right job type, the right duration, a technician with the right skills, a bay, a loaner if the rules allow one and a confirmation by text. It also moves, cancels and rebooks.

**Automated intake** collects what the workshop needs before the car arrives: license plate or VIN, mileage, symptoms in the customer's own words, photos of the damage or the warning light, contact preferences and consent, and confirms the drop-off time. For body shops it adds the claim number, the insurer and the photos the estimate needs.

Together they turn the sticky note into a job card that is already filled in.

## How booking automation works

1. The request comes in on any channel and the agent identifies the customer and the car, by phone number, plate or name.
2. It classifies the job. "Check engine light and sluggish" is a diagnostic. "Winter tires" is a seasonal swap with the stored set located.
3. It applies the workshop's rules: durations per job type, which technician does what, when loaners are offered, how breakdowns are prioritized.
4. It checks live availability in the calendar, planner or dealer system and offers two or three slots.
5. It writes the booking, reads it back before confirming and sends the confirmation by text.
6. It keeps the slot alive: a reminder the day before, a call within two hours if the customer does not show, and the waitlist worked down if a slot opens.

## How intake automation works

After the booking, the agent sends a short message or asks on the call: mileage, what the car is doing and when, a photo if useful. The answers go onto the job card. For a body shop, the claim number and photos reach the estimator before the customer does. At drop-off, the check-in is a confirmation, not an interview.

## The numbers behind it

- Most bookings still arrive by phone. CDK Global's survey of more than 2,500 service customers, published in 2025, found 64 percent booked by phone and 19 percent online. Automation has to cover the phone, or it covers a fifth of the demand.
- Customers want the option. In Cox Automotive's 2025 Service Industry Study, 71 percent rated scheduling service visits through a dealer's website or app as important. Far fewer had used it.
- The biggest frustration is time. 24 percent of dealership customers who had a frustration said service took longer than expected. Wrong durations at booking are a common cause.
- No-shows leak capacity. Vendor benchmarks such as AutoAlert's put dealership service no-shows at around 20 percent.
- Visuals sell the work. Cox found customers 49 percent more likely to approve recommended repairs when shown photos or video, which is why intake should collect them.
- Body shops have less slack than ever. Enterprise Mobility measured a 1.8-week scheduling backlog and a 16.3-day average collision rental in the first quarter of 2026, and CCC reports that 28.3 percent of repairable estimates now include calibrations.
- The volume is real. NADA's 2025 data shows the average US franchised dealership writing 16,252 repair orders a year, about 65 a working day, with 16 technicians.

## What good looks like

- Every booking has the right duration, technician and parts flagged before the car arrives.
- The customer says the symptom once, and it is on the job card.
- The estimator opens a claim that already has photos.
- A canceled Thursday slot is refilled by Wednesday evening.
- The counter checks cars in, instead of interrogating drivers.

## Pitfalls

- **Double bookings.** Insist on verified writes: the booking is read back from the planner before it is confirmed to the customer.
- **Vendor-set durations.** Durations, skills and loaner rules should be proposed from your own data and approved by the workshop manager.
- **Over-collection.** Ask only for what the job needs. GDPR applies to a photo of a license plate too.
- **Silent failures.** If the agent cannot take a call, it should ring through to the team, and that fallback should be tested at go-live.
- **No review loop.** Someone should read sampled calls every week and correct rules in plain language.

## Where to start

Start with booking on the phone, because that is where the volume is, and add intake once the bookings land correctly. At Nekaf, booking, reschedule and cancel are included in every plan, and the intake and check-in agent collects mileage, symptoms and photos before the visit and confirms the drop-off. Whatever you use, run it in shadow mode first and compare its bookings with the ones your team made the same week.

en.title: Call handling best practices for multi-site garage groups
en.description: Twelve practices for garage groups: one standard per site, pooled overflow, routing by intent, versioned rules, warm transfers and the numbers to compare.
en.body:
## Five sites, five phones

A regional manager opens Monday's report. Site A answered 91 percent of calls. Site D answered 63 percent. Site B has a greeting recorded by a receptionist who left last year. A customer who called site C to ask whether her car at site E was ready was told to call site E. Nobody knows how many calls went to voicemail on Saturday, because voicemail does not report.

Groups grow faster than their phone handling. Every acquisition brings its own line, its own habits and its own gaps. The practices below come from what works when a group decides to run the phone as one operation.

## Why it matters more for groups

Consolidation is the trend on both sides of the Atlantic. In US collision repair, Focus Advisors counted at least 4,019 locations under the five largest operators by mid-2025, about 13.3 percent of shops and 31.7 percent of revenue. Cox Automotive counts nearly 299,000 auto mechanic businesses in the US, up 12 percent since 2018. In Europe, the FIGIEFA and Roland Berger Panorama counts around 250,000 independent workshops and outlets, and chains keep adding sites.

Marchex, which analyzes calls for large multi-location automotive service operators, reports missed or failed call rates of up to 21 percent, with the best locations still near 10 percent. In a group, the gap between the best and worst site is the opportunity. And the phone is still the channel: 64 percent of service customers in a 2025 CDK Global survey booked by phone.

## Twelve practices

1. **Measure the same six numbers at every site.** Speed of answer, abandonment rate, booking accuracy, calls per advisor, after-hours volume and bay utilization. Weekly, per site, per hour of day. You cannot standardize what you do not compare.
2. **One standard, local detail.** The greeting, the escalation rules and the tone are the group's. Opening hours, technicians, stock and loaner cars are the site's. Keep both in one configuration so a change to the standard reaches every site at once.
3. **Route by intent and by site, not by which number was dialed.** A caller who reaches site C about a car at site E should get the answer, read from site E's planner.
4. **Pool the overflow.** When one site's counter is busy, the call should be answered somewhere, by a shared desk or a voice agent, rather than ringing out. A voice agent that reads every site's planner can answer fifty calls at once, and the difference between site A and site D disappears.
5. **Never voicemail.** After hours, a call should be answered and booked. Voicemail is where callers go to leave you.
6. **Write the breakdown rules down and version them.** Who is on duty at each site, what counts as urgent, what the driver is told. Every decision should carry the rule version that produced it.
7. **Transfer warm, with a summary.** A person picks up knowing the plate, the job and what the caller already said.
8. **Cut inbound with outbound.** Car-ready calls and texts the moment a job closes remove the most common inbound call at every site.
9. **Review sampled calls weekly, centrally.** One person reads flagged calls across all sites and corrects the rule once. A supervising review that scores calls on accuracy and tone makes this a half-hour job.
10. **One customer record.** A customer who uses two sites is one customer. Bookings, calls and summaries should land in one place, whatever the local planner is.
11. **Language per site.** English, Dutch, German or Spanish where the customers are, under the same rules.
12. **Roll out per site, with a shadow week.** Run the new handling on real calls without acting, compare it with what the site did, then switch on. Keep a pause button per site.

## What a group dashboard should show

- Answer rate and speed of answer, per site and per hour
- Bookings made and bay hours recovered, per site
- Breakdowns routed and time to reach a person
- Hand-offs and their reasons
- Sampled-call quality scores
- After-hours calls and what happened to them

## One group's experience

Broekema, a two-location garage group in the north of the Netherlands, had two lines, two greetings and two sets of gaps. After 5 PM and on Saturdays, calls went to a voicemail that only took messages. It forwarded both numbers to Nekaf on a Tuesday and went live on Thursday, with one standard for both sites, bookings into the right bay and breakdowns routed to the mechanic on duty with a summary. The planner integration followed later without interrupting the phones.

That order matters for groups: one standard first, integrations second, site by site.

## Questions to ask a vendor

- Can you show the same dashboard per site and for the group?
- Can a rule change go live for all sites at once, with a version number?
- Can I pause one site without touching the others?
- Where is the data held, and can it stay in the EU for my European sites?
- What happens to a call if your service is down?

en.title: The future of service booking in the automotive aftermarket

A driver sees an amber light on the dashboard on the way home from a weekend away. Today, the next step is waiting until Monday at 8 AM and calling a garage that is also opening its doors, checking in twelve cars and answering the parts window. Tomorrow, the booking is made on Sunday evening: by the driver on the phone with a voice agent, by the car itself, or by the garage's reminder agent that already knew the inspection was due.

ACEA counts 256 million passenger cars on EU roads with an average age of 12.7 years. S&P Global Mobility puts the US average at 12.8 years, the eighth consecutive annual rise. Older cars visit the workshop more often and for more complex work. Demand for service is not the problem for the next decade.

## Fewer people to do it

The TechForce Foundation estimates that US employers need about 241,842 new technicians a year through 2029 and that schools produce 101,743. Automotive alone: 70,000 openings, 42,000 graduates. Germany's ZDK has reported a shortfall of around 10,000 skilled workers. UWV counted 7,700 open vacancies in the Dutch car trade in mid-2026.

When capacity is the constraint, booking stops being a clerical task and becomes capacity management. Every no-show, every wrong duration and every unanswered call costs bay hours that cannot be bought back.

## Customers who still call, and expect more

Phone remains the main channel: 64 percent of service customers in CDK Global's 2025 survey booked by phone, 19 percent online. But expectations have moved. In Cox Automotive's 2025 Service Industry Study, 71 percent rated online scheduling through a dealer's website or app as important, 45 percent had a frustration with their last dealership visit, and the top frustration was that service took longer than expected. Cox's 2026 study found 16 percent of consumers already using AI tools somewhere in their service journey.

The channel is not going away. What changes is who answers it.

## Electrification changes the mix

Battery-electric cars took 17.4 percent of new EU registrations in 2025, according to ACEA, and 19.4 percent in the first quarter of 2026. In the Netherlands, 40.2 percent of new cars registered in 2025 were fully electric, according to BOVAG. Cox Automotive found EV owners take 67 percent of their service visits to a dealer, against 28 percent for combustion owners. Booking has to know which technician is qualified for high-voltage work and which bay has the equipment. That is a rules problem, and rules are what agents are good at.

2. **Booking that comes to you.** Reminders, recalls and seasonal tire swaps booked by an agent that works the vehicle list, rather than a call sheet on a Friday.
3. **A calendar that defends itself.** No-shows called within two hours, canceled slots refilled from a waitlist, durations corrected from what jobs actually took.
4. **Intake before arrival.** Mileage, symptoms and photos collected on the call or by message. Cox found customers 49 percent more likely to approve work when they see photos or video.
5. **The car as a caller.** Connected vehicles that report a fault and request a slot. Access to that data is still being argued over between manufacturers and the independent trade in both the EU and the US, and the outcome decides who gets the booking first.
6. **Proof before trust.** Shadow modes, supervising reviewers that score sampled calls, versioned rules and audit trails. In Europe the EU AI Act makes this expected rather than optional.
7. **Paying for outcomes.** Fees tied to bookings made and calls resolved rather than seats or minutes. Some vendors, Nekaf among them, already price this way, from $299 a month.

## What does not change

The customer at the counter still wants a person who knows the car. Diagnosis, warranty judgment and a difficult conversation stay human. The advisor's job shifts from answering the phone to using the time the phone used to take.

## What a workshop can do this year

## The third call about the same car

A body shop's front office, 2 PM. A customer calls to ask about her car. It is waiting on a door skin that was due yesterday. The estimator takes the call, looks it up, explains, apologizes. It is her third call this week. He has not finished an estimate since lunch. Two more calls are waiting.

Call burden is not a volume problem. It is a symptom of information that did not travel. The way to reduce it without lowering the standard of contact is to fix the reasons calls exist, answer the rest completely, and measure quality rather than assume it.

## Why the phone is heavier than it used to be

Repairs take longer and involve more steps. And the answers are inconsistent. Marchex, which analyzes calls for multi-location automotive service operators, puts missed or failed calls at up to 21 percent. In Cox Automotive's 2025 study, 45 percent of dealership customers had a frustration, and "service took longer than expected" led the list at 24 percent of them. Poor communication was one of the two main causes of dissatisfaction.

## Start by knowing what the calls are

Before changing anything, count. Tag a week of calls by reason. In one Dutch garage, 8,420 calls over two months broke down into three dominant reasons: general information, car-ready status and bookings. None of them needed a technician. ## Five strategies that work

1. **Remove the reason for the call.** Send the car-ready message the moment the job closes. Send the parts-arrived message. Send the estimate with photos and a link to approve. Cox found customers 49 percent more likely to approve work when they see photos or video, and a customer who has been told does not call to ask.
2. **Answer everything, resolve most.** A voice agent answers every call on the first ring, at any hour, and completes the routine ones end to end: hours, status, bookings, quotes read from the system. Nothing goes to voicemail, so nothing has to be called back.
3. **Route by need, with a summary.** Complaints, warranty questions and anything unclear go to a person who already knows the plate, the job and what the caller said. Quality goes up because the person only handles calls that need one.
4. **Protect the calendar.** Reminders the day before, a call within two hours of a no-show and a waitlist for canceled slots. Vendor benchmarks put dealership service no-shows around 20 percent, according to AutoAlert.
5. **Keep the number and the systems.** Forwarding on the existing line, integration with the existing planner or estimating system. No migration, no retraining.

Reducing calls can hide a falling standard if nobody checks. Track these every week:

- Answer rate and speed of answer, per hour
- Share of calls resolved without a person, and share handed off, with reasons
- Booking accuracy: right job, right duration, right technician
- Sampled-call scores on accuracy and tone, read by a manager
- Complaints and call-backs per hundred calls
- Time from job close to customer informed

en.title: Nekaf vs. Answering Services for Garages
en.description: Live answering services and Nekaf's voice agent compared for garages: what each does with a call, what it costs and when each one fits.
en.body:
It is 5:20 PM on a Thursday. The counter has gone home. A customer calls to ask whether his car will be ready in the morning. The answering service picks up in three rings, takes his name and number, and promises a call back. At 8:05 the next morning the counter finds the message, checks the planner and calls him. He is already on the bus.

That is the honest difference between an answering service and a voice agent. Both pick up. Only one of them answers.

## Quick comparison

| | Nekaf | Live answering service |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who answers | A voice agent trained on workshop calls | A human receptionist working from your script |
| Availability | 24/7, one caller or fifty at once | 24/7; capacity depends on staffing |
| Reads your planner | Yes, and writes bookings back | No, unless you share a calendar for simple slots |
| Car-ready status and quotes | Read from the planner and your price list | Message taken for a call-back |
| Breakdown handling | Your rules, transfer to the mechanic on duty with a summary | Message or transfer by script |
| Languages | English, Dutch and German | Depends on the provider and plan |
| Pricing | From $299 per month, tied to outcomes, no minutes | Plans by monthly minutes or per call, with overages |

## What an answering service does well

A live answering service gives you a human voice and a fast pickup. AnswerConnect says it answers 99 percent of calls within one to four rings. Ruby says it answers in under 10 seconds on average and serves more than 15,000 businesses. Both take messages, capture leads and, if you share a calendar, book simple appointments. For a business whose calls are mostly "please have someone call me", that is often enough, and some customers simply prefer a person.

## Where the message stops

A workshop's calls are not mostly "please call me back". They are "is my car ready", "what will the timing belt cost", "can I move Thursday to Friday" and "the engine light is on, can I still drive". Each needs your planner, your price list or your rules. A receptionist without those has to write it down. The caller waits for the call-back, the counter makes the call-back, and the busiest hour of the morning starts with yesterday's messages.

Marchex found up to 21 percent of automotive service calls at large operators unanswered, dropped or mishandled. CDK Global's 2025 survey of more than 2,000 service customers found four in ten ran into hold times, transfers, call-backs or no answer, and those whose call went unanswered gave a Net Promoter Score of 26.7, against an average of 59.

## What the minutes cost

Answering services sell time. Housecall Pro's July 2026 guide puts typical small-business plans at $135 to $400 a month, quotes $1.50 per minute and $2.50 per call as common examples, and warns that overages can run two to three times the base rate. AnswerConnect lists 200 minutes for $350 a month on its entry plan, with extra minutes at $2.50; Ruby prices its plans by monthly receptionist minutes. Car Wars data reported by CBT News in July 2026 puts the average service scheduling call at about four and a half minutes, so 200 minutes is roughly 44 booked appointments before overages. A tire-season week can use that up in days.

## How Nekaf differs

Nekaf answers on the first ring, in Dutch, German or English, and completes the call. It reads the planner, books the right job with the right technician and duration, tells the caller when the car is ready, reads back a quote, and follows the breakdown rules your workshop manager approved. Anything outside scope goes to a person with the transcript and a summary. Every call is written to the customer record.

Pricing does not count minutes. A monthly fee from $299 covers the agent, the console, unlimited users, setup and support, and follows the outcomes we agree up front. In a month with no results you pay nothing. Data is stored in the EU or the US. Most workshops are live within 48 hours on their existing number.

## Who should choose an answering service

- Workshops whose after-hours calls are rare and mostly messages
- Owners who want a human voice on every call, whatever it costs per minute
- Businesses with a simple calendar and no planner to read from

## Who should choose Nekaf

- Garages, dealerships, body shops and tire centers with peak-hour and after-hours volume
- Workshops that want bookings in the planner, not messages in an inbox
- Groups that need one standard across locations and an audit trail
- Owners who want to pay for booked jobs rather than minutes on hold

## Verdict

An answering service keeps the phone from ringing out. A voice agent keeps the customer from waiting. If most of your calls need your planner, your prices or your rules, Nekaf resolves them on the call and costs the same whether the week is quiet or it is the first frost of October.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can Nekaf take over from our answering service?

Yes. Forward the same number to Nekaf. It handles bookings, car-ready status, quotes and opening hours end to end and transfers the rest to your team with context. If Nekaf cannot take a call, it rings through to your team.

### Do customers mind talking to a voice agent?

Nekaf says who it is at the start of every call and moves to a person whenever the caller asks. At Autobedrijf van Nuland, more than six in ten calls were completed without staff and bookings rose 23 percent over 8,420 calls in May and June 2026.

Around the voice sit a Smart Inbox for calls and texts, LiveCSI, which flags unhappy customers while they are still at the dealership, and agents for advisor follow-ups, heat cases and declined work. Numa says it covers 90 percent of DMS installations and that most dealerships go live in two to three weeks.

## Where they differ

- Breadth. Numa's inbox, CSI monitoring and advisor agents go further into the service lane. Nekaf's agent library goes further into outcomes: reminders, no-show recovery, waitlist fills and quote follow-up.
- Oversight. Nekaf's shadow mode and the Reviewer show what the agent would do before it does it, and every decision is logged with its rule version.

## Who should choose Numa

- Dealerships in the United States or Canada that want one platform for calls, texts, CSI and advisor workflow

## Who should choose Nekaf

- Dealerships in the Netherlands or Germany, or groups with sites in Europe and the United States
- Groups that run both franchised stores and all-makes workshops
- Service managers who want a published, outcome-based price and a live agent within 48 hours

## Verdict

Numa is a strong choice for North American dealership groups that want the phone inside a broader service-lane platform. Nekaf is the choice when the service department is in Europe, speaks Dutch or German, runs alongside independent workshops, or wants pricing tied to booked jobs rather than a platform subscription. Numa's public materials describe dealerships in the United States and Canada. Nekaf was built for the Dutch, German and US markets and stores European data in the EU.
